title: If my friends change restaurants because of me, I'm being difficult.

original_metadata.statement: If my friends change restaurants because of me, I'm being difficult.
original_metadata.explanation: Having a medical dietary need does not automatically make you difficult. Friends may genuinely want to choose somewhere everyone can participate. You can also decide together what works for the group.
original_metadata.takeaway: Being included is not the same as being a burden.
original_metadata.source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: Bringing my own food is always the best solution.

original_metadata.statement: Bringing my own food is always the best solution.
original_metadata.explanation: Bringing food can be a useful backup, but it is only one strategy. Depending on the situation, you might research options, ask questions, eat beforehand, suggest another place, bring something, or combine approaches.
original_metadata.takeaway: Good self-management can look different in different situations.
original_metadata.source_organization: Celiac Disease Foundation + teen lived-experience extension

title: If I decide not to eat at a party, I failed at managing my celiac.

original_metadata.statement: If I decide not to eat at a party, I failed at managing my celiac.
original_metadata.explanation: Choosing not to eat can be a reasonable decision when you do not have enough information or do not feel comfortable. You can still participate socially.
original_metadata.takeaway: Success is not measured by whether you ate the food.
original_metadata.source_organization: Celiac Disease Foundation cross-contact guidance + teen lived-experience extension

title: I have to explain celiac disease to everyone who asks.

original_metadata.statement: I have to explain celiac disease to everyone who asks.
original_metadata.explanation: You can choose how much personal health information you want to share. Sometimes a detailed explanation helps; sometimes a short answer or boundary is enough.
original_metadata.takeaway: Self-advocacy includes deciding how much you want to explain.
original_metadata.source_organization: Teen self-management content; expert review required

title: Good self-advocacy can include saying, “No thanks.”

original_metadata.statement: Good self-advocacy can include saying, “No thanks.”
original_metadata.explanation: Self-advocacy is not only asking for accommodations. It can also mean politely declining food or a situation that does not work for you.
original_metadata.takeaway: You are allowed to say no without apologizing for having celiac disease.
original_metadata.source_organization: Celiac Disease Foundation + teen lived-experience extension

title: If a host worked hard to make something gluten-free for me, I should eat it so I don't hurt their feelings.

original_metadata.statement: If a host worked hard to make something gluten-free for me, I should eat it so I don't hurt their feelings.
original_metadata.explanation: You can appreciate someone's effort and still ask questions or decide not to eat. Gratitude does not require overriding your own food decision.
original_metadata.takeaway: You can be kind to the host and still make your own decision.
original_metadata.source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: If I've had celiac disease for years, I shouldn't need help anymore.

original_metadata.statement: If I've had celiac disease for years, I shouldn't need help anymore.
original_metadata.explanation: Experience can build skills, but it does not mean every situation becomes effortless. Planning fatigue, unfamiliar settings and social challenges can still happen.
original_metadata.takeaway: Independence can include knowing when to use support.
original_metadata.source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: My friends can be part of my celiac support system.

original_metadata.statement: My friends can be part of my celiac support system.
original_metadata.explanation: Friends can help in practical ways: planning together, learning about cross-contact, asking rather than assuming what works for you, or simply helping you feel included.
original_metadata.takeaway: Support does not have to come only from parents or healthcare professionals.
original_metadata.source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: Being independent with celiac means doing everything by myself.

original_metadata.statement: Being independent with celiac means doing everything by myself.
original_metadata.explanation: Independence means building your own decision-making and self-advocacy skills. It does not mean refusing help. Asking a friend, parent, server, teacher or healthcare professional for useful information can be part of managing celiac independently.
original_metadata.source_organization: Meyer & Naveh self-management framework; expert review required

title: Sometimes I can participate in a social event even if I decide not to eat there.

original_metadata.statement: Sometimes I can participate in a social event even if I decide not to eat there.
original_metadata.explanation: Sometimes eating is central to the event; other times the social connection matters most. Eating beforehand, bringing a backup, or simply joining friends without eating may be reasonable options depending on the situation.
original_metadata.takeaway: Participation does not always have to depend on eating.
original_metadata.source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: If everyone tells me a food is fine, that is the same as having enough information to decide for myself.

original_metadata.statement: If everyone tells me a food is fine, that is the same as having enough information to decide for myself.
original_metadata.explanation: Reassurance can feel helpful, but it may not answer questions about ingredients, preparation or cross-contact. You can decide what information you need.
original_metadata.takeaway: Reassurance and information are not the same thing.
original_metadata.source_organization: Beyond Celiac cross-contact guidance + teen lived-experience extension

title: If I've asked all the right questions and still feel nervous, I have to eat the food anyway or I'm letting celiac win.

original_metadata.statement: If I've asked all the right questions and still feel nervous, I have to eat the food anyway or I'm letting celiac win.
original_metadata.explanation: Plan My C-Day should never pressure you to eat. You can notice whether information is still missing, whether you are feeling uncertain, or whether you simply prefer another option.
original_metadata.takeaway: Confidence is not measured by forcing yourself to eat.
original_metadata.source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert/clinical review required

title: It's possible for foods I used to love to feel completely different after a celiac diagnosis.

original_metadata.statement: It's possible for foods I used to love to feel completely different after a celiac diagnosis.
original_metadata.explanation: A major dietary and health change can change how someone thinks or feels about food. Plan My C-Day does not label that reaction as good or bad. If food-related fear or avoidance is causing significant distress or limiting eating, support from a caregiver and celiac healthcare team may be helpful.
original_metadata.takeaway: Adjustment can be emotional as well as practical.
original_metadata.source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; clinical review required

title: If I'm tired of researching, checking and explaining, it means I'm bad at managing celiac.

original_metadata.statement: If I'm tired of researching, checking and explaining, it means I'm bad at managing celiac.
original_metadata.explanation: Knowing how to manage celiac does not mean the work never feels tiring. Using familiar options, sharing planning with others, or choosing a lower-effort strategy can sometimes reduce the mental load.
original_metadata.takeaway: Planning fatigue is different from not knowing what to do.
original_metadata.source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: Having celiac means I should always be the person teaching everyone else about it.

original_metadata.statement: Having celiac means I should always be the person teaching everyone else about it.
original_metadata.explanation: You can advocate when you want to, but having celiac does not make educating everyone your responsibility. Sometimes you may explain, share a resource, correct a misconception, or simply move on.
original_metadata.takeaway: Advocacy is an option, not another obligation.
original_metadata.source_organization: Teen self-management content; expert review required
